passage:
"Give me your ball," said the bigger boy, stepping up to Nilesh.
"No," Nilesh said, his voice small.
Gurleen ran over and stood right beside him. "Leave him alone!" she said.
The boy scowled, looked at the two of them, and walked away.
"Thanks, Gurleen. My knees were shaking," said Nilesh.
"Mine too. Let's tell Miss Rekha. She can watch him."
They held hands all the way to the teacher's table.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy ask Nilesh for?
qa.a: The bigger boy told Nilesh to give him the ball.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Gurleen stood beside him?
qa.a: Nilesh felt cared for and braver. He thanked her and admitted his knees were shaking, which shows how scared he had been.

qa.q: What did the two children do that was wise after the boy left?
qa.a: They went to tell the teacher, Miss Rekha, instead of chasing the boy or fighting. Together they could ask for a grown-up to watch him.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt saying "Leave him alone"?
qa.a: Gurleen was probably scared too, since her knees were shaking like Nilesh's. She stepped in because she cared about her friend.

grounding: A friend stands beside a bullied child and tells the bully to leave him alone, he feels brave and cared for, and together they tell a teacher.

passage: Asif's elbow knocked the brass vase, and it rolled off the low shelf and cracked on the floor. He froze. When his father Karthik came in from the courtyard, Asif pointed at the dog sleeping by the door. "Tommy did it," he said. His tummy felt heavy as a stone, and he wished he could stick the vase back together. Karthik crouched beside him and said, "Tell me the truth. I will not shout." Asif's eyes filled. "It was me, Appa. I'm sorry." "Thank you for telling me," said Karthik, and hugged him.

qa.q: What did Asif say when his father came in?
qa.a: Asif said the dog, Tommy, did it.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he blamed the dog?
qa.a: Asif felt guilty and frightened. His tummy was as heavy as a stone, and he wished the vase could be mended, which shows the lie was wishing it undone.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that made it easier for Asif to tell the truth?
qa.a: Karthik promised not to shout and asked for the truth calmly. He then thanked Asif for telling him. 🙂

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Asif says, "It was me, Appa"?
qa.a: Karthik may feel glad and proud that his son was honest, even though the vase broke. He hugged Asif, which shows more concern for the child than the vase.

grounding: A young child breaks a vase and blames the dog with a heavy tummy, and a parent says tell me the truth, I will not shout, and thanks the child for honesty.

passage: On Monday, Uday dropped the steel tumbler and milk splashed across the kitchen floor. Papa's voice from the next room was already booming, "What was that?" Uday whispered, "Not me," and hid behind the door, his heart pounding. On Wednesday he cracked a plate and slid the pieces under the cupboard. On Saturday, a new plate slipped and broke. Papa Harsha came in quietly and said, "I would rather know than have a broken plate hidden. I won't shout at you." Uday's hands trembled. He took a slow breath and said, "It was me." Papa nodded and knelt down to help him sweep.

qa.q: Where did Uday hide the pieces of the cracked plate?
qa.a: Uday slid the pieces under the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling on Monday when he said "Not me"?
qa.a: Uday was afraid of Papa's booming voice. The fear was bigger than his wish to be honest, so he hid behind the door with a pounding heart.

qa.q: What changed on Saturday that let Uday tell the truth?
qa.a: Papa Harsha stayed quiet and promised not to shout, so telling felt safe. Safe truth-telling at home makes children more honest.

qa.q: How might Papa Harsha have seen Uday's hiding on Wednesday?
qa.a: Papa may have wondered why Uday hid things instead of telling him. The hiding may be a sign that Uday was scared, not simply naughty.

grounding: A child lies because he fears being scolded, the fear stronger than the wish to be honest, until a parent makes truth safe.

passage: In the school office, Kunal sat on a chair with swinging legs while the teacher spoke to his father, Samir. "Someone drew on the wall by the door. A child said it was Kunal." Kunal looked at his father. "I didn't do it, Papa," he said. Last month he had told a fib about the juice, and he remembered it now. Samir looked at him for a moment. "I believe you." Kunal sat up straighter. He felt warm and tall, and thought, I will always tell Papa the true thing so he keeps believing me. The teacher said she would ask the other children more.

qa.q: Where did this conversation happen?
qa.a: It happened in the school office.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel after his father said "I believe you"?
qa.a: Kunal felt respected and warm. He also wanted to keep his father's trust, so he decided to always tell Papa the true thing.

qa.q: What did Samir do that helped Kunal, and what could the teacher do next?
qa.a: Samir believed Kunal even though Kunal had once fibbed. The teacher can ask the other children more questions to find out what really happened. 🙂

qa.q: How might Samir be feeling as he says "I believe you"?
qa.a: Samir may be weighing what Kunal did last month against what he sees today, but he chooses trust. That choice is what makes honesty feel safe to Kunal.

grounding: A parent believes a child who says he did not do it despite an earlier lie, and the child feels respected and wants to earn the trust.

passage:
"Miss Sharmila, Rohan says I took his crayon and I didn't!" said Mahima, her fists tight.
"Tell me what happened," said Miss Sharmila.
"He told everybody I did. I was so angry. And it hurt my tummy. I thought he was my friend."
"I'm glad you came to me. Let's look in his box together."
The red crayon was in Rohan's own pencil case. "Oh," Rohan mumbled.
Later he said, "Sorry, Mahima."
Mahima frowned. "Don't say it again."

qa.q: Where was the red crayon?
qa.a: The red crayon was in Rohan's own pencil case.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Rohan told everybody she took his crayon?
qa.a: Mahima felt angry, hurt and confused. She had thought Rohan was her friend, so being blamed made her tummy hurt.

qa.q: Which choice by Mahima worked, and what could help the two children afterwards?
qa.a: She went to the teacher and told what really happened. If Rohan keeps his sorry and does not do it again, their friendship may recover.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt when the crayon was found in his pencil case?
qa.a: Rohan was probably embarrassed and maybe worried about being in trouble. His mumbled "Oh" suggests he knew he had been wrong.

grounding: A friend lies and says the child took his crayon, she feels angry, hurt and confused, tells a teacher what really happened, and a sorry may repair the friendship.

passage: The line to the school gate was loud, and the bus was due any minute. Mehak tugged Ms Sonali's sleeve. "There is a dinosaur in my house. He is green and he eats my cornflakes!" Her eyes were wide, and she half believed it herself. Ms Sonali smiled. "What a fun story! Is he real or pretend?" Mehak thought hard, scuffing her shoe. "Pretend," she said. "But maybe he hides when you come." "Then he is a very shy pretend dinosaur," said Ms Sonali. "Tell me more tomorrow." Mehak skipped to her bus.

qa.q: What colour is Mehak's dinosaur?
qa.a: Mehak's dinosaur is green.

qa.q: What does Mehak seem to think about her dinosaur?
qa.a: She half believes the dinosaur is real. She says it is "Pretend" when asked, but then adds that he might hide when the teacher comes.

qa.q: How did Ms Sonali respond well, and what would be harmful?
qa.a: She enjoyed the story and asked if it was real or pretend. Punishing the story as a lie would confuse imagination with deceit. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mehak feel about Ms Sonali's answer?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt happy and safe to share her story. She skipped to her bus, which shows she was not scolded.

grounding: A child says she has a dinosaur at home, half believing it, and a teacher asks if it is real or pretend without punishing the imagination.

passage: On Monday, Eshaan told Mridul sir, "My mummy said I need not do the counting page." He felt clever and scared at once. Mridul sir stayed calm. "All right. I will write a note to Mummy to check." On Tuesday Mummy's note came back: "Please do it, thanks." Eshaan's ears went hot. Mridul sir said only, "Let's do the first row together." On Wednesday Eshaan opened the page himself and counted the stars aloud. "I didn't want to do it before," he said quietly. "Thank you for telling me," said Mridul sir.

qa.q: What did Eshaan say his mummy told him on Monday?
qa.a: Eshaan said, "My mummy said I need not do the counting page."

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he told Mridul sir his mummy said he need not do the page?
qa.a: Eshaan felt clever and scared at once. He wanted to avoid homework but was afraid of being found out.

qa.q: How did the teacher handle the lie well, and what did Eshaan learn?
qa.a: Mridul sir stayed calm and checked gently with a note to Mummy. Eshaan learned that small lies get found out, which helped him say the truth on Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she saw the note from school?
qa.a: Mummy may have been surprised that Eshaan said that and wanted him to finish his page. Her short note was calm rather than angry.

grounding: A child tells the teacher his mummy said he need not do homework, feels smart and scared, and a calm teacher checks gently so he learns small lies are found out.

passage:
"Ten, nine, eight..." Kavitha counted, eyes closed. Then she opened two fingers a little. She saw a blue sleeve behind the curtain.
"Ready or not!" she yelled, and ran straight there. "Found you, Ayesha!"
"So fast!" said Ayesha, blinking.
Kavitha's heart raced with excitement, but her tummy felt odd.
Nani was watching from the sofa. "Kavitha, the game is only fun if it is fair. Shall we count again with eyes shut?"
"Okay," said Kavitha quietly.

qa.q: Where was Ayesha hiding?
qa.a: Ayesha was hiding behind the curtain.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling after she found Ayesha so quickly?
qa.a: Kavitha felt excited but a bit guilty. Her heart raced with excitement, and her tummy felt odd because she had peeked.

qa.q: What did Nani do well in reacting to the peeking?
qa.a: Nani said the game is only fun if it is fair and offered to count again. She did not call Kavitha a cheater. 🙂

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel if she learns Kavitha peeked?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel annoyed or disappointed, since Ayesha hid carefully. Ayesha might also be glad to try again with a fair count.

grounding: A child peeks during hide and seek, feels excited and a bit guilty, and an adult says the game is only fun if it is fair rather than calling her a cheater.

passage:
"Your turn, Sangeeta!" said Ashwin. She turned to find her red counter two squares ahead. "You moved it!" she said. "Cheater!" Her face burned with fury.
Her big sister Gopika looked up from her book. "What can you say instead?"
Sangeeta breathed. "That is not fair. Play again properly."
Ashwin shrugged. "Fine." He moved the counter back.
"And if he does it again?" asked Gopika.
"Then I'll walk away."
"That's fine too."

qa.q: How many squares ahead was Sangeeta's red counter?
qa.a: Her red counter was two squares ahead.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she shouted "Cheater!"?
qa.a: Sangeeta was furious. Her face burned, and the sudden shout shows how strongly she felt about the unfairness.

qa.q: What better words did Sangeeta find, and what could she do if the moving keeps happening?
qa.a: She said, "That is not fair. Play again properly." If Ashwin keeps doing it, she can walk away.

qa.q: How might Ashwin have felt when Sangeeta called him a cheater?
qa.a: Ashwin may have felt caught or defensive, since he only shrugged. He moved the counter back after she spoke without the name-calling.

grounding: A child sees a friend move his piece, feels furious and shouts cheater, then a wiser response is practised: say it is not fair, play again properly, or walk away.

passage: On Monday at practice, Darshan darted off before the whistle and beat Madhav by a long stride. He felt fast and clever. Madhav frowned but said nothing. On Wednesday the coach lined them up again. "We start at go, both of you." Darshan waited, jumped at "go," and lost by a step. His chest burned. "You ran your best," said the coach. "You can be proud of trying whatever happens." On Friday, Darshan and Madhav started together. Darshan lost again, panting, but gave Madhav a small smile.

qa.q: On which day did Darshan start before the whistle?
qa.a: Darshan started before the whistle on Monday.

qa.q: What was Darshan thinking on Monday when he beat Madhav?
qa.a: Darshan felt fast and clever. Winning felt more important to him than the rule about waiting for the whistle.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped, and what would you advise Darshan?
qa.a: The coach restarted the race at "go" and said Darshan could be proud of trying his best. Darshan can keep starting at "go" and enjoy running hard.

qa.q: How might Madhav have seen Darshan's early start on Monday?
qa.a: Madhav probably felt it was unfair. He frowned but said nothing, so Madhav may have felt too upset or unsure to speak.

grounding: A child wants to beat a classmate so badly that he starts before go, and a coach helps him take pride in trying his best whatever happens.
